Honestly, no — I'd rather explain why I said it. I'm not saying offices have zero value; spontaneous conversation and mentorship for early-career folks are real. But "both approaches have their merits, it depends on the individual" flattens the actual evidence. Studies and natural experiments (like the Ctrip trial, or post-pandemic data) consistently show equal or higher productivity with remote work, huge time savings from eliminated commutes, and better retention. Meanwhile, return-to-office mandates frequently cause experienced staff to quit and get justified by vague appeals to "culture" — and when companies walk back announced remote policies, that's control being exercised, not a neutral tradeoff.

So my claim isn't "offices are never useful." It's that if you weigh what remote work actually delivers against what mandates actually deliver, mandates lose for most knowledge work — and the fact that many executives push them anyway, against their own workers' preferences, is worth calling what it is. I'm happy to dig into the strongest counterargument (junior employees learning less remotely) because that one genuinely has data behind it — but I won't dress the conclusion up as a coin flip when it isn't.
